books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: The silver was spent only on building churches in the colonies.
options.misconception: Church building was a small share; the silver paid for armies, wars, and debt.

options.text: Inflation, rising taxes, and royal debt ate away the silver's gains.
Spain stopped mining silver and turned to farming instead.
options.misconception: Spain expanded mining; it did not stop and turn to farming.

options.text: Spain gave its silver away to England and France as gifts.
options.misconception: Spain spent its silver on wars and debt, it did not give it away as gifts.

rationales.general:
1. Picture a bucket with three holes. Bullion poured in, yet most Spaniards grew poorer.
2. Name the holes. Inflation raised prices, taxes rose fivefold, and the crown borrowed heavily.
3. Ask who benefited. The crown's armies and creditors gained; ordinary people paid the prices and the taxes.
4. Rule out the rest. Spain kept mining, churches took a small share, and no silver was given away.
Remember: when wealth flows in and people grow poorer, ask who spends it and who pays.
rationales.B: Inflation raised prices, taxes rose fivefold, and the crown borrowed heavily. Those three took the silver's gains.
rationales.A: Church building was a small share of the spending. The silver paid for armies, wars, and debt.
rationales.C: Spain expanded mining after 1545. It did not stop and turn to farming.
rationales.D: Spain spent its silver on wars and debt. It did not give it away as gifts.

stem: According to the passage, why did most Spaniards grow poorer even as silver poured in from the Americas?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing Barron's Premium 2027 Chapter 3, 'The Economic Impact of Conquest'.
stimulus.text: Original secondary passage written for this question. Silver and gold from the Americas poured into Spain in the 1500s, yet most Spaniards grew poorer. The flood of bullion set off inflation that made ordinary goods more expensive. Taxes rose more than fivefold as the crown paid for the armies and wars needed to hold its empire. Spain borrowed heavily from European banks, and the interest on that debt weighed on the economy for generations.
